topic: Classes: constructors, init order & backing fields

questions.question: What does this print?
options:
prop a
init 1
prop b
init 2

init 1
init 2
prop a
prop b

prop a
prop b
init 1
init 2
questions.explanation: Property initializers and `init` blocks are merged into the primary constructor and run top to bottom in declaration order. `init` blocks are not run as a group before or after the properties.

questions.question: What happens when you compile and run this?
questions.explanation: Without `val` or `var`, `name` is only a constructor parameter. It can be used in initializers and `init` blocks but is not a property, so member functions can't see it. Write `class User(val name: String)` to make it a property.

questions.question: If a class has a primary constructor, every secondary constructor must delegate to it, either directly with `: this(...)` or through another secondary constructor.
questions.explanation: Kotlin requires this so the primary constructor's initializers and `init` blocks always run. A secondary constructor without `: this(...)` in a class with a primary constructor is a compile error.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The delegation `: this(name)` runs first, which runs the primary constructor with all `init` blocks. Only after that does the secondary constructor's own body run.

questions.question: What happens when `main` runs?
options: Compile error: `name` cannot be assigned inside its setter
`name` becomes ` Ann ` because the setter is skipped
questions.explanation: Inside the setter, `name = ...` calls the setter again, so it recurses forever. It compiles (with at most a warning). To store the value, assign the backing field: `field = value.trim()`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `totalOnce` has an initializer, so it is computed once at construction (when `count` is 0) and stored. `total` has a custom getter and no backing field, so it is recomputed on every read.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The override is dispatched virtually, so `Child.describe()` runs. But `Base`'s init runs before `Child`'s property initializers, so `label` still holds the JVM default `null`, even though its type is non-null `String`.

questions.question: Given this ViewModel property, what can code outside the class do with `count`?
options: Read it, but not assign it
Assign it, but not read it
questions.explanation: `private set` keeps the getter public and makes only the setter private. Outside code can read `vm.count` but `vm.count = 5` is a compile error, so all changes go through `increment()`.

questions.explanation: The argument to the superclass constructor is evaluated first, then the parent constructor runs fully (its init blocks), and only then the child's initializers and init blocks run in declaration order.

questions.question: For `class BadgeView(context: Context, attrs: AttributeSet? = null) : View(context, attrs)`, Java code (such as the XML inflater looking up constructors) only sees the two-argument constructor unless you add `@JvmOverloads constructor`.
questions.explanation: Default arguments are a Kotlin-side feature: the JVM gets one constructor taking all parameters (plus a synthetic one). `@JvmOverloads` generates the extra overloads, which is why custom Views often use `@JvmOverloads constructor(...)`.

questions.question: Why does this Hilt repository need the `constructor` keyword, when `class UserRepository(private val api: UserApi)` normally doesn't?
options: `constructor` is required when the primary constructor has annotations or modifiers
It turns the primary constructor into a secondary constructor that Hilt can call
`private val` constructor parameters are only allowed with an explicit `constructor` keyword
It makes the constructor `public` so Hilt can reach it
questions.explanation: The keyword can be omitted only when the primary constructor has no annotations or modifiers. To put `@Inject` (or `private`) on it, you must write `constructor`. It is still the primary constructor, and it is already public by default.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: A property initializer writes straight to the backing field and does not call the custom setter, so `level` starts at 50. The later assignment goes through the setter and is clamped to 10.

questions.question: Which declarations let code outside the class read `User("Ann").name`? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: `val`/`var` in the primary constructor declare public properties, and a body property initialized from the plain parameter works too. A plain parameter alone isn't a property, and `private val` is a property that outside code can't see.

questions.question: Inside a regular member function, you can write `field` to read or write a property's backing field directly, bypassing its getter and setter.
questions.explanation: `field` is only available inside that property's own getter or setter. In other member functions the name means nothing special, and you access the property through its accessors.

questions.question: This class has no primary constructor. What does this print?
questions.explanation: `Logger()` delegates to `Logger(String)`. That constructor has no `this(...)`, so it runs the initializers and `init` blocks in order, then its own body. Control then returns to the no-arg constructor's body.

questions.question: In `var title: String = ""; set(value) { field = value.uppercase() }`, what is `field`?
options: The property's backing storage, usable only inside its accessors
A keyword that declares a new private property
The previous value of `title`, passed into the setter as a read-only copy
A reference to the object, like `this`
questions.explanation: `field` refers to the property's backing field. Assigning `field` stores the value without calling the setter again. It is not a new property, and it can be written to, unlike a read-only copy.

questions.question: This custom View is inflated from XML. What happens?
options: It works, because all properties are initialized before any `init` block
Compile error: `paint` must be declared before `init`
It works, but the color is reset when `paint` is initialized
questions.explanation: Initializers and `init` blocks run in declaration order, so `paint` is still `null` when `init` calls `applyColor`. The compiler only catches direct references to a later property, not ones that go through a function call. Fix it by moving `paint` above the `init` block.

questions.explanation: The named argument sets only `port`, so `host` falls back to its default `localhost`. Named arguments let you skip earlier parameters that have defaults.

questions.question: What happens when you compile and run this?
options: Prints `2`, because the body property shadows the constructor one
questions.explanation: `val id` in the constructor already declares a property, so the body declaration is a redeclaration. A body property can reuse the name only when the constructor parameter is a plain parameter without `val`/`var`.

questions.question: Which of these properties have a backing field? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A backing field exists if the property uses a default accessor or an accessor that mentions `field`. `b` and `e` have custom accessors that never touch `field`, so they have no storage and cannot take an initializer.
